questions.title: What standard does the Fifth Circuit use when reviewing a district court’s denial of Judgment as a Matter of Law (JMOL) on infringement?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Wi‑LAN, Inc. v. Apple Inc. for de novo review. I’m trying to understand whether the court still checks whether the evidence is substantial, or if the de novo review replaces that requirement. How exactly does the court evaluate ‘substantial evidence’ in the context of JMOL versus a factual finding?

questions.title: How does the court distinguish between an interference generating signal that is 'generated' versus 'sampled', and why does that matter for claim limitation 1[a] of the ’134 patent?
questions.question_body: The decision focuses on whether the RF ADC samples the modeled PIM path. I’m confused about the technical distinction between a signal that is generated by the hardware after sampling and one that is present in the passband being sampled. Why does the court say the modeled PIM path cannot be the 'interference generating signals' if it’s produced after sampling?

questions.title: What does it mean for an expert’s testimony to be 'self‑contradictory' under the standard in Johns Hopkins Univ. v. Datascope Corp., and how was that applied to Dr. Wells’ testimony in this case?
questions.question_body: The opinion says Dr. Wells’ testimony was confusing and contradictory, yet it references a single platform—his sources x1 and x2—without mapping them to the required signals. How does the court determine that a jury could not have relied on such testimony?

questions.title: Why did the court hold that Finesse did not successfully surrender claim scope over two signals when it amended the claims to recite ‘three signals’?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Cont’l Circuits LLC v. Intel Corp. as a basis for not treating the amendment as a clear disavowal. I’m unsure how claim amendments are evaluated for scope surrender, especially when the amended claims specify a numeric limitation that seems to exclude the prior art’s two‑signal approach.

questions.title: What is the significance of the court’s analysis of the seven third‑order multiplications in the ’775 patent, and how does the lack of a mapping to the Nokia document’s operations affect the infringement verdict?
questions.question_body: The opinion discusses how Dr. Wells relied on a Nokia document that listed only three multiplications. I’m not clear on why showing that the accused device performs ‘any’ of the seven multiplications is insufficient for infringement when the court says the device must perform *all* of them. How does the claim wording enforce that requirement?

questions.title: On what basis does the Fifth Circuit vacate a damages award after reversing a JMOL ruling, and what rules govern that process?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that reversing the JMOL decision automatically necessitates vacating the damages award. I’d like to understand the procedural logic and any statutory or case law that obligates the appellate court to vacate damages when infringement is found non‑infringing.
